# PlainLang principles

Why the rules exist, with the evidence behind them.

## P01 Know the reader and what they need to do

Clear writing starts before the first sentence: decide who will read it, what they already know, and what they must do afterward.

- Picture one real reader; Buffett wrote SEC filings as if to his two smart, non-expert sisters.
- Plan for the reader's task: find, understand, use.
- Assume the reader knows less than you think. Pinker calls the gap the curse of knowledge.

**Caveat:** Pinker notes that empathy alone doesn't fix this: people are poor at guessing what others don't know, so test with readers.

**Rules:** CLR-01, CLR-08, CLR-09, CLR-15

**Sources:** [SEC, A Plain English Handbook (1998)](https://www.sec.gov/pdf/handbook.pdf); [Federal Plain Language Guidelines](https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language); [Pinker, The curse of knowledge (APS Observer)](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/observer/the-curse-of-knowledge-pinker-describes-a-key-cause-of-bad-writing)

## P02 Put the main point first

Lead with the conclusion, answer, or required action. Background follows.

- U.S. Army correspondence standard: bottom line up front (BLUF).
- Web readers scan; NN/g recommends the inverted pyramid.
- ClearMark judges praised an opening statement of purpose and required action.

**Evidence:** In Kimble's survey of 251 Michigan lawyers, 61% preferred the plain-language judicial opinion; an opening summary was one of the top reasons.

**Rules:** ORD-01, ORD-03, CLR-15

**Sources:** [BLUF / Army Regulation 25-50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLUF_(communication)); [Kimble, Michigan Bar Journal (2016)](https://www.michbar.org/file/barjournal/article/documents/pdf4article2972.pdf); [2026 ClearMark winners](https://centerforplainlanguage.org/awards/clearmark/2026-clearmark-awards-winners/)

## P03 Make characters subjects and actions verbs

The clearest sentences tell a small story: who did what. Put the actor in the subject and the action in the verb.

- Diagnose: compare the sentence's subject and verb with the story's real character and action.
- Turn hidden verbs (analysis, management, application) back into verbs.
- Prefer active voice when the actor matters.
- Zinsser: find the people behind the product or story; real people are more compelling than abstract nouns.

**Caveat:** Nominalizations can name real abstractions (Sword). The passive is right when the actor is unknown or irrelevant (GOV.UK). Pullum showed that Strunk & White misidentified most of their 'passive' examples, so check before 'fixing'.

**Rules:** ACT-01, ACT-02, ACT-03, ACT-04, ACT-05

**Sources:** Williams & Bizup, Style: Lessons in Clarity and Grace; [Sword, Zombie Nouns (NYT, 2012)](https://yale-nus.edu.sg/academics/wp-content/uploads/sites/8/2021/12/Nominalizations-Are-Zombie-Nouns-The-New-York-Times.pdf); [Federal Plain Language Guidelines](https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language/writing); [Zinsser, On Writing Well, ch. 16 (LitCharts)](https://www.litcharts.com/lit/on-writing-well/chapter-16-business-writing-writing-in-your-job)

## P04 Meet the reader's structural expectations

Readers expect context at the start of a sentence and emphasis at the end, and the verb soon after the subject.

- Put the verb right after the subject.
- Start with old, linking information; end with the new.
- Keep each paragraph's topics consistent (topic strings).

**Caveat:** Gopen and Swan present these as expectations a writer can break for effect, not rules.

**Rules:** CLR-02, CLR-03, WORD-04, ORD-07

**Sources:** [Gopen & Swan, The Science of Scientific Writing (1990)](https://wstomv.win.tue.nl/quotes/science-of-scientific-writing.html); Williams & Bizup, Style

## P05 Use short, familiar words

Choose the everyday word your reader would use: buy, help, about, start.

- Orwell's rule 2: never use a long word where a short one will do.
- GOV.UK and 18F publish words-to-avoid lists (utilize, facilitate, leverage, deliver for abstract things).
- Use the words your users search for.
- The federal guidelines publish a 'dirty dozen' to replace first: addressees, assist, commence, implement, in accordance with, in order that, in the amount of, in the event of, it is, promulgate, this activity, utilize.
- Zinsser's clutter list: 'personal friend', 'at the present time', 'assistance' for help, buzzwords, 'I might add'. CDC's Everyday Words maps about 100 public-health terms to everyday ones.

**Evidence:** Oppenheimer's five experiments (Applied Cognitive Psychology) found readers judged writers who used needlessly complex words as less intelligent.

**Caveat:** The target is needless complexity. Precise technical terms are fine when the reader knows them or you define them.

**Rules:** CLR-07, WORD-02, WORD-06, WORD-07, WORD-10, WORD-12

**Sources:** [Orwell, Politics and the English Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_and_the_English_Language); [GOV.UK clear language](https://guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk/writing-to-gov-uk-standards/writing-guidelines/clear-language/); [18F plain language](https://guides.18f.org/content-guide/our-approach/plain-language/); [Readability Guidelines: words to avoid](https://readabilityguidelines.netlify.com/clear-language/words-to-avoid/); [Federal Plain Language Guidelines: Use simple words and phrases (archived)](https://web.archive.org/web/2023/https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/words/use-simple-words-phrases/); [CDC Everyday Words](https://www.cdc.gov/other/pdf/EverydayWordsForPublicHealthCommunication.pdf)

## P06 Keep sentences and paragraphs short

One idea per sentence, one topic per paragraph.

- GOV.UK: split sentences over 25 words; no more than 5 sentences per paragraph.
- Microsoft: bigger ideas, fewer words.
- Federal guidelines: one idea per sentence; paragraphs of no more than 150 words in three to eight sentences, never over 250.
- Sentence targets vary by source: Simply Put 8-10 words; Flesch 15 (conversational) to 20 (plain); HHS, usability.gov, and STE instructions 20; GOV.UK, Mailchimp, and STE descriptions 25. Paragraphs: HHS 3 lines on the web; Simply Put 3-5 sentences; usability.gov and STE 6 or fewer.

**Evidence:** In the studies Kimble reports, preferred plain versions averaged 18 to 19 words per sentence, down from about 25.

**Caveat:** Length is a proxy. A long sentence that is a simple list can read easily. NIH's Clear & Simple warns that writing to a readability formula can produce choppy text and drop useful familiar words.

**Rules:** ORD-02, CLR-14, ORD-05, FILL-07

**Sources:** [GOV.UK clear language](https://guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk/writing-to-gov-uk-standards/writing-guidelines/clear-language/); [Microsoft Writing Style Guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/style-guide/top-10-tips-style-voice); [Kimble (2016)](https://www.michbar.org/file/barjournal/article/documents/pdf4article2972.pdf); [Federal Plain Language Guidelines: Write short paragraphs (archived)](https://web.archive.org/web/2023/https://www.plainlanguage.gov/guidelines/concise/write-short-paragraphs/); [HHS Health Literacy Online 2.6](https://odphp.health.gov/healthliteracyonline/2016/write/section-2-6/); [usability.gov guidelines ch. 15](https://webarchive.library.unt.edu/eot2008/20080916213614/http:/usability.gov/pdfs/chapter15.pdf); [Flesch, How to Write Plain English, ch. 2](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~wstarbuc/Writing/Flesch.htm)

## P07 Be concrete and specific

Name the thing, the number, the person. Go down the ladder of abstraction.

- SEC ladder: asset, investment, security, equity, stock, common stock, one share of IBM common stock.
- Give an example for every abstract claim (Pinker).
- Pinker's classic style: write as if pointing at something the reader can see.

**Rules:** CLR-06, CLR-09, WORD-03, WORD-05, WORD-13

**Sources:** [SEC Plain English Handbook](https://www.sec.gov/pdf/handbook.pdf); [Pinker (APS Observer)](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/observer/the-curse-of-knowledge-pinker-describes-a-key-cause-of-bad-writing)

## P08 Be concise, scannable, and objective

Cut words, make text easy to scan, and drop promotional tone.

- Concise: about half the words.
- Scannable: headings, lists, highlighted keywords, one idea per paragraph.
- Objective: no marketing claims.

**Evidence:** Morkes and Nielsen (1997) tested 51 users on five versions of a travel site. Against a promotional control, overall usability was 58% better for the concise version (about half the words), 47% for scannable, 27% for objective, and 124% for all three combined. A later rewrite of real Sun web pages scored 159% better.

**Caveat:** For the objective-only version, only the satisfaction gain was statistically significant; task time, errors and memory improved but not significantly. The scannable version scored slightly lower than the control on memory. It is one 1997 study on one small site.

**Rules:** FILL-07, FMT-05, WORD-10, CLR-14

**Sources:** [Morkes & Nielsen, Concise, SCANNABLE, and Objective (NN/g, 1997)](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/concise-scannable-and-objective-how-to-write-for-the-web/)

## P09 Speak to the reader: you, present tense, positive

Address the reader directly, describe how things work now, and say what is true rather than what isn't.

- Use 'you' (Google, plainlanguage.gov).
- Present tense is simplest; limit conditionals.
- Use 'must' for requirements, 'can' for options; avoid 'shall'.
- Turn negatives into positives (SEC).

**Rules:** CLR-01, CLR-04, CLR-05, CLR-10, ACT-03

**Sources:** [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style/highlights); [Federal Plain Language Guidelines](https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language/writing); [GOV.UK clear language](https://guidance.publishing.service.gov.uk/writing-to-gov-uk-standards/writing-guidelines/clear-language/)

## P10 Write for global readers

Plain, literal English translates and survives non-native reading.

- Avoid idioms, slang, and culture-bound references (seasons, holidays, sports).
- Keep helper words: that, then, of.
- Put conditions before instructions.
- Use one term per concept.
- Keep optional words (that, the, then) and repeat verbs and subjects for clarity (Microsoft, Mailchimp).
- Avoid -ing and -ed words whose role is ambiguous (Microsoft, Mailchimp, STE).
- Choose words with one meaning: because, not since; after, not once (Microsoft, Mailchimp).
- Controlled languages like ASD-STE100 go further: about 900 approved words, one meaning each.

**Rules:** CLR-13, CLR-21, WORD-11, WORD-01, WORD-09

**Sources:** [Google: Write for a global audience](https://developers.google.com/style/translation); [Microsoft: Global writing tips](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/style-guide/global-communications/writing-tips); [Mailchimp: Writing for translation](https://styleguide.mailchimp.com/writing-for-translation/); [Simplified Technical English (Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Technical_English)

## P11 Design for the task

Layout is part of clarity: headings that say what's in the section, numbered steps, tables for comparisons, checklists for actions.

- Use numbered lists for steps and bulleted lists for other parallel items.
- Use headings that describe content.
- ClearMark judges repeatedly praise headings, white space, and a 'quick takeaway' at the top.

**Caveat:** Over-structuring short answers is its own fault (see FMT-05).

**Rules:** CLR-11, CLR-12, FMT-03, FMT-04, FMT-05, CLR-19, CLR-20

**Sources:** [2026 ClearMark winners](https://centerforplainlanguage.org/awards/clearmark/2026-clearmark-awards-winners/); [Google style highlights](https://developers.google.com/style/highlights)

## P12 Test with real readers, not formulas

The only reliable test of clarity is whether readers can find, understand, and act on the text.

- Use paraphrase testing, usability testing, or the plus-minus technique.
- Test early and at least twice.
- If you can't reach real readers, ask someone unfamiliar with the topic to read aloud and explain.
- NIH: one comment that reveals a misunderstanding of a key concept deserves attention, since others may share it silently.
- NIH: test comprehension, attractiveness, and acceptability; never rely on expert review alone.

**Evidence:** Jarrett reports a study where formula-driven edits lowered scores by up to six grade levels without improving comprehension.

**Caveat:** Treat this rule set's regex hits the same way: as prompts to look, not verdicts.

**Rules:** CLR-18

**Sources:** [digital.gov: Test for understanding](https://digital.gov/guides/plain-language/test); [Jarrett, Readability formulas: seven reasons to avoid them](https://www.effortmark.co.uk/?p=3586); [NIH Clear & Simple](https://www.nih.gov/institutes-nih/nih-office-director/office-communications-public-liaison/clear-communication/clear-simple)

## P13 Treat guidelines as guidelines

Every rule here has exceptions. Clarity for this reader beats compliance with a list.

- Orwell's sixth rule: break any of these rules sooner than say anything barbarous.
- Gopen and Swan: reader expectations can be broken deliberately.
- Linguists (Pullum, Liberman) warn that mechanical style rules misfire.

**Sources:** [Orwell, Politics and the English Language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_and_the_English_Language); [Language Log, The redemption of zombie nouns](https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=4095); [Pullum, The Grammarians Have No Clothes](https://www.wilsonquarterly.com/quarterly/_/the-grammarians-have-no-clothes/)

## P14 Make it actionable

Clear isn't enough if the reader can't act. Say what to do, how, and why it's worth doing.

- Give one main message and a call to action (CDC CCI items 1, 5).
- Break behaviors into small steps the reader can start now (HHS 2.5).
- Explain why each step matters and what the reader gains (CCI 13; HHS 2.4).
- Stay positive: focus on tips for overcoming barriers, not the barriers (HHS 2.4).

**Evidence:** HHS cites self-efficacy, a person's belief they can succeed, as a strong predictor of health behavior; small steps and relatable stories build it.

**Rules:** CLR-16, CLR-05, ORD-01

**Sources:** [CDC Clear Communication Index](https://www.cdc.gov/ccindex/tool); [HHS Health Literacy Online, Write](https://odphp.health.gov/healthliteracyonline/2016/write/); [CDC Simply Put](https://cdc.gov/health-literacy/pdf/Simply_Put.pdf)

## P15 Plain language is relevant, findable, understandable, usable

The ISO standard defines plain language by outcomes for the reader, not by word lists.

- Relevant: readers get what they need.
- Findable: they can easily find it.
- Understandable: they can easily understand it.
- Usable: they can easily use it.
- Only about 7% of the standard's roughly 485 ideas are about word choice; most are about structure, findability, and design.

**Caveat:** The full standard is paywalled; this summary comes from the federation that drafted it.

**Rules:** CLR-15, CLR-19, CLR-20

**Sources:** [International Plain Language Federation: ISO 24495-1](https://www.iplfederation.org/the-iso-plain-language-standard-part1)

## P16 Present numbers people can use

Numbers inform only when readers can interpret them without math.

- Use whole numbers and natural frequencies ('1 in 4').
- Explain what each number means: high or low, better or worse than expected.
- Do conversions and calculations for the reader; keep denominators constant.
- Prefer absolute risk to relative risk; explain any probability in words or a visual.

**Rules:** CLR-17

**Sources:** [CDC Clear Communication Index, Part C-D](https://www.cdc.gov/ccindex/tool); [CDC Simply Put](https://cdc.gov/health-literacy/pdf/Simply_Put.pdf)

## P17 Score drafts with a checklist

A checklist makes clarity reviewable. CDC's Clear Communication Index is a research-based example: 20 yes/no items, passing score 90 out of 100.

- Core (all materials): one main message; at the top; visually emphasized; a supporting visual; a call to action; active voice in the main message; everyday words; lists; chunks with headings; key information first; uncertainty acknowledged.
- Behavior (when asking for action): a recommendation; why it matters; how to do it.
- Numbers: familiar forms; meaning explained; no math required.
- Risk: nature of the risk; risks and benefits; probabilities explained in words.
- Before writing, answer five planning questions: audience, audience research, objectives, format and channel, pretesting plan.

**Evidence:** CDC developed the Index from research literature and expert review for public-facing materials.

**Caveat:** Written for public health materials; items like 'supporting visual' don't apply to chat replies.

**Rules:** ORD-01, CLR-16, CLR-17, CLR-18, CLR-08

**Sources:** [CDC Clear Communication Index user guide](https://Cdc.gov/ccindex/pdf/clear-communication-user-guide.pdf)
